Recognizing a Sketch
While It Is Being Drawn

A recurrent neural network (GRU) on Google's Quick, Draw!

Marco Cavazza

Data and problem

  • Quick, Draw! (Google): doodles drawn in 20 seconds
  • A sketch is not an image but a sequence of pen points (Δx, Δy, pen lifted)
  • 10 classes, ≤ 100 points per sketch
    100k train / 23.6k validation / 23.5k test
  • Goal: after every point t, estimate

    the answer changes while the sketch grows
point tΔxΔypen

Δx, Δy: pixels from the previous point  ·  pen = 1: end of a stroke

Proposed architecture

  • Input: one point at a time, xt = (Δx, Δy, pen)
  • 2 GRU layers, memory of 128 numbers
  • Linear + softmax: class probabilities after every point
  • Loss: cross-entropy at every real point (padding masked out)

The building block: the GRU cell

  • Reset gate rt: how much of the past to use for the new content
  • Update gate zt: how much of the memory to overwrite
  • Candidate h̃t: new content from the current point
  • New memory ht: mix of old memory and candidate, a summary of the strokes so far

The network while a cat is being drawn

Conclusions

  • A GRU reads a sketch as a sequence of pen points and recognizes it among 10 classes with 95.5% test accuracy (logistic regression baseline accuracy: 54%)
  • It gives an answer after every point: with half of the sketch it is already right 88% of the time (baseline accuracy: 24%)
  • Its errors are between similar shapes (clock ↔ pizza)
  • A drawing treated as a process in time, not as a static image: the idea behind online handwriting recognition (e.g. Google's keyboard) and sketch models like Sketch-RNN (Ha & Eck, 2017), trained on Quick, Draw!
